Rules summary Contents 1 Objective 1.1 Turn Structure 1.2 Available Cards 1.3 Card Types 1.3.1 Item Cards 1.3.2 Special Item Cards 1.4 Opening Additional Escape Pods 1.5 Playing Face-Down Cards 1.6 Successfully Loading a Pod 1.7 Jamming an Escape Pod 1.7.1 If Only One Pod Exists 1.7.2 If Multiple Pods Exist 1.8 LAUNCH! 1.9 Winning the Game Objective Be the first player to empty your stash by successfully loading all of your belongings into escape pods. Turn Structure On your turn: Choose an escape pod. Play 1 available card onto it. Players normally may only play 1 card per turn unless instructed otherwise by a special card. Available Cards A card is considered available if no other card overlaps or covers it in your stash. Covered cards cannot be played until uncovered. Card Types Item Cards Have a numeric value. To play successfully, the card value must be equal to or greater than the top card currently on the chosen escape pod. Special Item Cards Have special effects instead of numbers. Can generally be played on any pod. Resolve their instructions immediately when played. Opening Additional Escape Pods If a player has a Keycard: At the start of their turn, they may open a new escape pod. Discard the Keycard from the game. Place a new pod face-up beside the others. Immediately play a card onto the new pod. There must always be at least one escape pod available. Playing Face-Down Cards Face-down cards remain hidden when uncovered. To play one: Choose a pod. Flip the card over while playing it. Resolve the result normally. This may cause a jam. Successfully Loading a Pod A numbered card successfully loads if its value is: Equal to the top card value, or Higher than the top card value. Jamming an Escape Pod If a player places a numbered card lower than the top card on the pod, the pod jams. When a pod jams: Take all cards from that pod, including the card that caused the jam. Shuffle those cards. Refill empty spaces from the player’s stash that existed at the start of the turn. Fill the bottom row first. All replacement cards are face-up. Discard any leftover cards. If Only One Pod Exists Leave the pod in play after clearing it. If Multiple Pods Exist Remove the emptied pod from the game after refilling the stash. LAUNCH! Some special cards contain the LAUNCH! effect. After resolving the card’s instructions: Discard the entire escape pod and all cards on it from the game. If no pods remain afterward: Place a new unused pod into play. Winning the Game The first player to successfully play their final card and completely empty their stash wins immediately.

---

"Family Values? Nah, Family Valuables!" You and 2-10 greedy relatives were living it up on the galaxy’s finest space station—until a fire turned your vacay into a screaming, stuff-grabbing frenzy! The rescue shuttle’s pods are here, but in Relative Space, it’s every family member for themselves. Hurl your ukulele in to nix their sock monkey—because nothing beats the glee of screwing over your family mid-catastrophe. It’s a chaotic blast of ensuring your items make it on the pods as you battle to save your loot. First to pack everything jets off triumphant, waving bye-bye to the flaming rubble and their tears!

In Relative Space, each player has a pile of 12 cards representing their valuables, with the 5 cards at the bottom of the pile facedown. In turn order, players must play one card to an available escape pod. The card played must be clear of cards on top, and should be of equal or high value than the top card in the escape pod. First player to pack all 12 of the cards in front of them wins!

—description from the publisher

[Rating: 3/10] Having open hands kinda feels anathema to shedding games. You don't have much choice due to your hand being in a pyramid a la 7W Duel and I felt like it played on auto-pilot.  A little bit of decision space around screwing the next player when they have no specials and you can play high to block any available non-jamming plays for them.  Just didn't see the point.

[Rating: 4/10] Party-ish card playing game with take-that elements, but overall trying get rid of your pyramid of cards before your opponents do that. Turns usually are quite obvious with not much thinking involved.

[Rating: 4/10] After a few rounds on BGA: This is a rather mindless shedding game that you can play on autopilot, much like Uno. In many turns, there is really only one sensible thing to do. Sometimes, there is literally only one possible move. That feels too shallow for a modern game design, especially if the game isn’t explicitly marketed as a children’s game. Despite having about the same level of strategic depth as Uno, its rules are more complicated.  Interestingly, I found the first few games quite entertaining.
